package.title: 総括 — 2026年夏の到達点と残る設計課題
package.editorial_angle: 本文各章で分解した物理配置、計算資源、network fabric、service/data contract、open platform、development lifecycle、安全・セキュリティを再び一枚のE&E設計像へ統合する。『centralize everything』ではなく、責務をどこに置き、何を契約として固定するかが2026年時点の本質的な設計課題であると結論づける。
must_cover: physically zonal / computationally centralized の再確認
Ethernet中心だが単一busではない
ECU境界からservice/data/resource contractへの移行
software development/validation infrastructureもE&E architectureの一部
安全・セキュリティ・determinismが中央集約の実効上限を決める
標準仕様・OSS実装・OEM/Tier1実装の間に残る検証gap
boundaries: The authors frame the interview analysis as qualitative rather than statistically significant; findings therefore should not be treated as population-level quantitative validation.
The practitioner interview study is tied to Daimler Truck AG and the paper discusses external-generalizability limits; architecture conclusions should be treated as contextual rather than universal.
Which detailed mandatory/optional TSN feature selections and configuration parameters are normative in the full IEEE Std 802.1DG-2025 text?
This verification used public IEEE project/publication pages; detailed normative requirements and parameter values in the full standard were not independently inspected.
VSS specifies a vehicle-data taxonomy/model and associated tooling; these releases do not by themselves establish a transport protocol, service runtime, or OEM-wide adoption.
Statements such as 'production-ready' or predictable/safe behavior are project claims unless backed by separate certification, conformance or deployment evidence.
The evaluation is a laboratory setup using TurtleBots, ESP32-based ECU emulation and a central backend, not a production vehicle/fleet validation.
The authors explicitly identify deployment to a larger connected-vehicle testbed and deeper feature-model/variant-management integration as future work.

For simplicity, the model assumes coexistence/freedom-from-interference criteria are satisfied when mixed-criticality tasks share hardware; the optimization does not itself establish the complete safety argument for that coexistence.
Scalability experiments use a fixed four-ECU architecture with randomly generated task graphs and randomized WCET/WCRT/cost values, limiting direct transfer to a production E/E program.
Reported objective values and solver timings are case-study/problem-instance results rather than universal design-space optimization performance.

artifact.canonical_name: Centralization potential of automotive E/E architectures
artifact.organization: Daimler Truck AG / Technical University of Munich / University of Stuttgart

sources.title: Centralization potential of automotive E/E architectures (arXiv:2409.10690)
sources.role: Author preprint and metadata establishing methodology summary, criteria and author claims.

sources.title: Centralization potential of automotive E/E architectures — Journal of Systems and Software
sources.role: Publisher page and article text/snippets used to verify research-method and threats-to-validity statements.

claims.text: The authors identify seven evaluation criteria for centralization potential: busload, functional safety, computing power, feature dependencies, development and maintenance costs, error rate, and modularity/flexibility.
The study combines a literature review with qualitative interviews of practitioners at Daimler Truck AG; the interview analysis is qualitative and explicitly not aimed at statistical significance.
claims.context: Methodological description from the paper/publisher text.

claims.text: The authors report centralization as a key SDV enabler while also warning that centralization can shift rather than eliminate complexity, and that some strict functional-safety needs may still favor local embedded ECUs.

metrics.name: centralization evaluation criteria count
metrics.context: Author-defined set derived from literature review and used in the qualitative study.

limitations.text: The authors frame the interview analysis as qualitative rather than statistically significant; findings therefore should not be treated as population-level quantitative validation.
The practitioner interview study is tied to Daimler Truck AG and the paper discusses external-generalizability limits; architecture conclusions should be treated as contextual rather than universal.

targets.target: Verify the architecture, evaluation setup, material claims and limitations reported for Centralization potential of automotive E/E architectures; preserve paper results as AUTHOR_CLAIM unless independently established.
targets.finding: The primary paper/publisher text confirms the literature-review plus qualitative-interview design, the seven criteria, architecture framing, qualitative-analysis boundary and threats-to-validity discussion. Claims remain AUTHOR_CLAIM rather than independent validation.

editorial.why_now_note: Published during the 2023-2026 transition window, the paper directly addresses when centralization is beneficial and when local/distributed constraints remain.
editorial.rationale: It provides a useful architecture-decision framework and explicit anti-monolith/safety caveats, complementing standards and implementation evidence.

sources.title: P802.1DG – TSN Profile for Automotive In-Vehicle Ethernet Communications
sources.role: Official IEEE 802.1 project page establishing scope, publication status, approval/publication dates and project history.

sources.title: Publication: IEEE 802.1DG-2025 Time-Sensitive Networking Profile for Automotive In-Vehicle Ethernet Communications
sources.role: Official IEEE 802.1 publication announcement summarizing automotive TSN profile purpose and applicability.

claims.text: IEEE 802.1DG is a published 2025 standard; the project page records Board approval on 2025-05-28 and publication on 2025-06-06.
claims.context: Status/date evidence from the IEEE 802.1 project page.

claims.text: The standard defines an automotive in-vehicle Ethernet TSN profile for bridged IEEE 802.3 networks, addressing deterministic/bounded latency and selecting applicable IEEE 802.1 TSN/security features for automotive use.
claims.context: Publicly stated standard scope; detailed normative parameters were not inspected.

claims.text: The public IEEE summary positions 802.1DG as guidance for automotive vendors/suppliers designing in-vehicle networks with bounded latency, bandwidth and synchronization requirements.
claims.context: Architecture relevance follows the standard’s stated profile purpose.

limitations.text: This verification used public IEEE project/publication pages; detailed normative requirements and parameter values in the full standard were not independently inspected.

targets.target: Verify the official scope/status and architecture-significant statements on ieee-8021dg-automotive-tsn; distinguish directly checkable facts from organization/project claims.
targets.finding: Official IEEE 802.1 pages establish published-standard status, approval/publication dates, and the automotive TSN profile scope. Detailed normative contents remain outside this verification.

unresolved_questions: Which detailed mandatory/optional TSN feature selections and configuration parameters are normative in the full IEEE Std 802.1DG-2025 text?

editorial.why_now_note: Publication in 2025 places a formal automotive TSN profile inside the 2023-2026 E/E transition window.
editorial.rationale: A published automotive-specific TSN profile is directly relevant to deterministic Ethernet as the network substrate for centralized/zonal E/E architectures.

sources.title: Eclipse S-CORE
sources.role: Pinned official project-page snapshot used to verify platform scope, layering, code-first orientation and current stated release-gate status.

claims.text: The S-CORE project page states that it targets software-platform layers above the SoC board-support package and below the application layer, spanning OS abstraction, middleware and application-level services.
The page explicitly describes S-CORE as code-first, with executable code, tests, CI and reference implementations rather than only a paper standard.
The page identifies hardware/software decoupling, modularity and project-specific extensibility as platform goals.
The pinned page snapshot states that S-CORE had reached release gate v0.8 and describes stronger requirements/architecture/safety-artifact expectations for modules in scope for v1.0.
claims.context: Direct page content at the pinned observation time; not equivalent to safety certification.

limitations.text: Statements such as 'production-ready' or predictable/safe behavior are project claims unless backed by separate certification, conformance or deployment evidence.

targets.target: Verify the official scope/status and architecture-significant statements on eclipse-score-project; distinguish directly checkable facts from organization/project claims.
targets.finding: The pinned project page provides direct evidence of S-CORE's intended stack boundaries, code-first delivery model and current project-status language; safety/production claims remain project claims.

editorial.why_now_note: S-CORE is a concrete shared runtime/platform effort that directly reflects the shift from proprietary per-OEM core stacks toward common automotive software infrastructure.
editorial.rationale: Strong platform-level candidate when combined with release-series evidence and explicit maturity caveats.

artifact.canonical_name: An OpenSource CI/CD Pipeline for Variant-Rich Software-Defined Vehicles

sources.title: An OpenSource CI/CD Pipeline for Variant-Rich Software-Defined Vehicles
sources.role: Author arXiv paper/preprint used to verify the architecture, evaluation scope, material claims, and limitations available in the primary text.

claims.text: The proposed open-source pipeline structures SDV software into development, build/test, artifact storage and deployment stages, with variant metadata driving target-specific artifacts across ECUs, HPCs and backend systems.
A cloud/client OTA middleware pair selects compatible versions from artifact metadata, delivers updates to heterogeneous targets, verifies them and supports rollback/telemetry.

The laboratory evaluation demonstrates variant-specific firmware updates/rollback on emulated ECUs, Snap-based vehicle-control updates, and containerized AI-model deployment to TurtleBot/ROS 2 targets with a backend.

metrics.name: TurtleBots used in AI evaluation
metrics.context: One designated as the Ego TurtleBot for model deployment.

metrics.name: embedded-software vehicle variants evaluated
metrics.context: Variant-specific OTA packages and rollback were tested on two ECU configurations.

limitations.text: The evaluation is a laboratory setup using TurtleBots, ESP32-based ECU emulation and a central backend, not a production vehicle/fleet validation.
The authors explicitly identify deployment to a larger connected-vehicle testbed and deeper feature-model/variant-management integration as future work.

targets.target: Verify the architecture, evaluation setup, material claims and limitations reported for An OpenSource CI/CD Pipeline for Variant-Rich Software-Defined Vehicles; preserve paper results as AUTHOR_CLAIM unless independently established.
targets.finding: The full primary text verifies the variant-aware CI/CD/OTA architecture, ECU/HPC/backend target model, rollback, two embedded variants, three-TurtleBot AI test, and larger-testbed/variant-management future-work boundary.

editorial.why_now_note: SDV architecture extends beyond runtime ECUs: software provenance, target compatibility, OTA, rollback and variant management become part of the vehicle system architecture.
editorial.rationale: Direct evidence for cloud-to-vehicle software lifecycle architecture, including variant derivation, OTA delivery, rollback and multiple deployment target classes.

artifact.canonical_name: ASIL-Decomposition Based Resource Allocation Optimization for Automotive E/E Architectures

sources.title: ASIL-Decomposition Based Resource Allocation Optimization for Automotive E/E Architectures
sources.role: Author paper/preprint used to verify the reported architecture, method/evaluation scope, material claims, and limitations available in the primary text.

claims.text: The authors formulate automotive software-to-hardware mapping, scheduling and ASIL decomposition as a single mixed-integer linear optimization problem targeting development cost and critical-chain execution time while applying safety/reliability constraints.

The exemplary case study exposes a cost/latency trade-off: prioritizing development cost yields lower cost with longer maximum application execution time, while prioritizing latency increases cost and reduces that execution time.
The authors compare Gurobi and CPLEX and report that solving time grows as task count increases; ASIL decomposition cases can materially increase optimization time.
claims.context: Generated/evaluated problem instances, not production design-cycle measurements.

limitations.text: For simplicity, the model assumes coexistence/freedom-from-interference criteria are satisfied when mixed-criticality tasks share hardware; the optimization does not itself establish the complete safety argument for that coexistence.
Scalability experiments use a fixed four-ECU architecture with randomly generated task graphs and randomized WCET/WCRT/cost values, limiting direct transfer to a production E/E program.
Reported objective values and solver timings are case-study/problem-instance results rather than universal design-space optimization performance.

targets.target: Verify the architecture, evaluation setup, material claims and limitations reported for ASIL-Decomposition Based Resource Allocation Optimization for Automotive E/E Architectures; preserve paper results as AUTHOR_CLAIM unless independently established.

editorial.why_now_note: Resource allocation under ASIL and timing constraints is a direct mechanism by which centralized/mixed-criticality E/E architecture choices become computable rather than intuitive.
editorial.rationale: Strong design-method evidence if solver/cost/latency values remain tied to the exemplary case study and FFI assumption.
